solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Fit mock rings with unknown gems (9)

indicatorNotes.rings: to ring something is to circle it, so JEER goes round WELL

blocks.note: x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns

annotation.surface: A jeweller sneers at a tray of fake rings set with stones nobody can identify.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fit" and "mock" both read as adjectives in the surface, but mock is a verb (jeer) and fit means healthy.
annotation.definitionFit: Gems set in rings and necklaces are jewellery.

entries.clue: Candy corporation trousers altered by Spooner (5,5)

indicatorNotes.altered by Spooner: Dr Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds change places

blocks.note: a corporation is an old jokey word for a paunch
swap the B and J sounds

annotation.surface: A sweet company's uniform trousers get a makeover from someone called Spooner.
annotation.walkthrough: "Corporation" looks like a business beside "Candy"; here it is the old slang for a pot belly.
annotation.definitionFit: Jelly beans are sweets, which Americans call candy.

entries.clue: Nuns use these glues regularly to stop drips (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters at even steps
indicatorNotes.to stop: the letters plug the gap inside WIMPS, like a stopper

blocks.note: a drip is a feeble person, a wimp

annotation.surface: Convent handywomen reach for adhesive to seal leaks.
annotation.walkthrough: "Drips" reads as leaks; it means feeble people. A wimple is the cloth headdress framing a nun's face.
annotation.definitionFit: The wimple is the headdress nuns traditionally wear.

entries.clue: Game wrecked after losing bishop (5)

indicatorNotes.after losing: the word has to lose the letter named

blocks.note: wrecked and blotto are both slang for very drunk
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop; it is removed

annotation.surface: A player's game falls apart once the bishop is lost, as in chess.
annotation.walkthrough: The chess picture makes "wrecked" sound like a ruined position; it is slang for drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance with numbered cards.

entries.clue: Jumbo jet uncovered in the plane compound (11)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: strip off the outer letters, leaving the middle
indicatorNotes.compound: a compound is a mixture, so the letters are mixed

annotation.surface: A jumbo jet parked inside an aircraft compound.
annotation.walkthrough: "Jumbo jet" reads as one phrase, but it splits: Jumbo is the definition and jet the wordplay. "Compound" sounds like an enclosure; it means mixture.
annotation.definitionFit: Jumbo and elephantine both mean enormous; Jumbo was a famous circus elephant.

entries.clue: Give up rabbit (3)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom

blocks.note: to give money is to pay

annotation.walkthrough: "Give up" wants to be one phrase meaning surrender. In British slang to rabbit (on) is to chatter endlessly, and so is to yap.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal use: to rabbit on is to chatter tiresomely, and the other word is equally informal for noisy chatter.

entries.clue: Crop a former PM’s broadcast (5)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: something broadcast is heard, so go by the sound

blocks.note: Theresa May was UK Prime Minister 2016 to 2019

annotation.surface: An ex-Prime Minister's interview is cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: "Crop" looks like a verb, to cut the broadcast; it is the noun, a harvest.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this cereal, also called corn, is one of the world's main field crops.

entries.clue: Odd climbing gear worn by Earl’s killer (9)

indicatorNotes.climbing: in a down clue, climbing reads the word upwards
indicatorNotes.worn by: the Earl wears the dress, so it goes round him

blocks.note: rum is British slang for odd

annotation.surface: An eccentric outfit for a mountaineering aristocrat.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture is of strange climbing kit; "climbing" is really the instruction to flip RUM.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is general: the answer is one particular kind of killer, a woman who has committed murder.

entries.clue: Popular measures for auditors making cuts (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer is a verb, 'incises', where the definition is the participle phrase

indicatorNotes.for auditors: auditors are listeners, so the word is judged by its sound

annotation.surface: Accountants taking a well-liked approach to reducing spending.
annotation.walkthrough: "Auditors" and "cuts" build an accounts picture; auditors here are simply listeners.
annotation.definitionFit: To incise is to cut into something.

entries.clue: Fish lists at Billingsgate (4)

indicatorNotes.at Billingsgate: Billingsgate is London's fish market, where a Cockney accent drops the H

blocks.note: a ship that lists heels over; the H goes

annotation.surface: Stall price lists at London's fish market.
annotation.walkthrough: Billingsgate is London's historic fish market, so a Cockney porter says 'EELS for heels. "Lists" looks like price lists; it is leaning over.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain class name: these snake-like creatures are fish, and jellied ones are a Cockney speciality, which suits Billingsgate.

entries.clue: Motorway enclosed by illuminated verge (5)

indicatorNotes.enclosed by: the first word sits inside the second

blocks.note: the M1, written MI, is the classic crossword motorway

annotation.surface: A motorway with floodlit grass verges.
annotation.walkthrough: The roadside verge is a false trail: here verge means an edge or boundary.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of edge or boundary, the point beyond which you cannot go.

entries.clue: Awful crime pal and I observed (9)

indicatorNotes.Awful: an awful version of the letters is a bad, jumbled one

annotation.surface: A witness admits seeing a dreadful offence alongside an accomplice.
annotation.walkthrough: "Observed" reads as a verb, what the pair saw; it is an adjective, based on observation.
annotation.definitionFit: Empirical knowledge is observed rather than theorised.

entries.clue: Chicken beats other birds (13)

blocks.note: chicken and yellow both mean cowardly
to beat soundly is to hammer

annotation.surface: A farmyard hen sees off rival birds.
annotation.walkthrough: "Chicken" is a bird too, hence "other birds" in the definition, but here it means cowardly. Yellowhammers are small yellow buntings.
annotation.definitionFit: Yellowhammers are birds, other than the chicken just mentioned.

entries.clue: Tipsy medic using a wrong direction (11)

indicatorNotes.Tipsy: the letters stagger about like a drinker

annotation.surface: A drunken doctor sends someone the wrong way.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a doctor's bad advice, which is exactly what the answer means.
annotation.definitionFit: A near-literal gloss: the prefix mis- means wrong and guidance means direction.

entries.clue: Ravel concert’s finale in lifeless Bordeaux? (10)

indicatorNotes.finale: a finale is the closing part of a show, so take the word's closing letter
indicatorNotes.in: the concert's finale is placed in the next word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: Bordeaux is one example of wine, hence the question mark

annotation.surface: A performance of the composer Ravel ends with flat claret.
annotation.walkthrough: Ravel wants to be the French composer, which fits concert and Bordeaux; it is the verb. To ravel means to tangle, not only to unravel.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though a surprising one: ravel originally means to tangle threads together, the opposite of what most people assume.

entries.clue: Record store new in Greek capital, possibly (7)

annotation.surface: A new record shop opening in Athens.
annotation.walkthrough: "Greek capital" wants to be Athens; it is a capital letter of the Greek alphabet, and "possibly" admits epsilon might be lower case.
annotation.definitionFit: Epsilon is a Greek letter, capital E among its forms.

entries.clue: Duck’s tail hurt after gents step on it (4,5)

indicatorNotes.tail: a tail is the back end of an animal, so take the back end of the word
indicatorNotes.after: what follows comes after the first piece

blocks.note: the gents is a men's toilet, a loo
to smart is to sting, to hurt

annotation.surface: A duck is hurt when some men tread on its tail.
annotation.walkthrough: "Step on it" seems to be the men treading on the duck; it is the idiom for hurry up. Look smart is British for be quick.
annotation.definitionFit: Look smart and step on it both mean hurry up.

entries.clue: Second mate’s boy comes aboard (7)

blocks.note: the son of a second husband or wife
to come aboard a bus is to get on it with a stride; split the letters 5,2

annotation.surface: A second mate on a ship brings his lad on board.
annotation.walkthrough: The second mate is a ship's officer in the surface; in the answer it is a second marriage partner.
annotation.definitionFit: A stepson is the son of one's second mate; someone boarding steps on.

entries.clue: Toff — one that keeps feeling capital! (7)

indicatorNotes.that keeps: the outer word holds the inner one

blocks.note: a nob or toff is an upper-class person
an air is a feeling or atmosphere

annotation.surface: An upper-class type exclaims that it all feels splendid.
annotation.walkthrough: "Capital!" is a toff's cry of approval in the surface; it is the city, capital of Kenya. A toff is a posh person.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the answer is one capital city, Kenya's.

entries.clue: Establish how a monarch passed on lies (7)

annotation.definition2: how a monarch passed on lies

blocks.note: to establish someone is to install them in a post

blocks.clueFragment: how a monarch passed on lies
blocks.note: a dead king or queen is laid out with ceremony so the public can pay respects; split the letters 2,5

annotation.surface: Proving how a king spread falsehoods.
annotation.walkthrough: "Passed on lies" reads as spreading falsehoods; it means died and is lying. A monarch lies in state before the funeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: the verb means to install in office, and read as two words it is the ceremonial lying of a dead monarch.

entries.clue: Draw spotlight away from winning coach (7)

blocks.note: a team that is up is ahead
a stagecoach, so a stage is a coach

annotation.surface: A victorious manager is upstaged by his own publicity.
annotation.walkthrough: "Coach" reads as a sports trainer; it is the horse-drawn vehicle, a stage.
annotation.definitionFit: A theatre idiom: an actor who moves upstage makes a colleague face away from the audience, stealing the spotlight.

entries.clue: Sanitised, like Troy in the Iliad, say (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: the Iliad is an example of an epic poem

annotation.surface: Troy, as Homer's epic portrays it, has been sanitised.
annotation.walkthrough: Troy is the city in Homer's Iliad in the surface; the wordplay only wants its abbreviation T, from troy weight.
annotation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free of germs, sanitised.

entries.clue: One paying to receive American tan lingerie (9,4)

indicatorNotes.to receive: the outer word takes the other inside

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat, belt, them

annotation.surface: A shopper paying for an American's tan-coloured underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: "Tan" reads as a colour of stockings; it is the verb, to thrash.
annotation.definitionFit: A suspender belt is an item of women's underwear that holds up stockings.

entries.clue: Engineers left computers fired up again (5)

annotation.surface: Technicians left the computers to reboot.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fired up" suggests switching a computer on; here it is lighting a fire again.
annotation.definitionFit: Something relit has been set alight again.

entries.clue: Theatre incomplete without female company (4)

blocks.note: the stage means the theatre as a profession; drop the E

annotation.surface: An unfinished play staged with no women in the cast.
annotation.walkthrough: A stag party or stag night is a men-only celebration before a wedding.
annotation.definitionFit: Stag describes an all-male occasion, without women.

entries.clue: Open-air café of note next to a grand forest (3,6)

blocks.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
the Forest of Arden, from As You Like It

annotation.surface: A notable outdoor café beside a great forest.
annotation.walkthrough: "Of note" reads as famous; it is the musical note TE. "Grand" looks like an adjective for the forest; it is G.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: the answer names a garden where refreshments are served outdoors, which is what an open-air café is.

entries.clue: Money mostly for parties (3)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word: drop its last letter

blocks.note: dosh is British slang for money; the H goes

annotation.surface: Cash spent largely on partying.
annotation.walkthrough: A do is a British word for a party, and dosh is British slang for money.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal use: a do is a party or social function, and the plural matches parties.

entries.clue: Sort of hilt round a heavy Indian club (5)

indicatorNotes.Sort of: a sorted, rearranged version of the letters
indicatorNotes.round: the rearranged letters go round A

annotation.surface: A sword hilt wrapped around an Indian weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: A lathi is the long iron-bound bamboo stick carried by Indian police.
annotation.definitionFit: A lathi is a heavy stick used as a club in India.

entries.clue: Huge jar in the auditorium (5)

indicatorNotes.in the auditorium: an auditorium is where things are heard

blocks.note: to jar is to grate on the nerves

annotation.surface: An enormous jar standing in a concert hall.
annotation.walkthrough: "Jar" reads as a pot; it is the verb, to grate.
annotation.definitionFit: Great and huge both mean very large.

entries.clue: In retrospect, a clean World Cup, perhaps (9)

indicatorNotes.In: the answer is inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: Looking back, a World Cup free of scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: "Perhaps" marks the World Cup as just one example of a spectacle.
annotation.definitionFit: A World Cup is a grand public show, a spectacle.
